priya.name: Dr. Priya Nair
priya.role: materials scientist (someone who studies what things are made of and how they behave)

case.title: Kai’s Treasure Pouch
case.hook: Dr. Priya Nair here. It’s the morning after Campfire Night. Kai panned the creek at sunrise (he swirled creek sand in a pan, hunting for gold) and came back with a pouch of treasure! He tied a tag on every find. But Kai only LOOKED at them. What is each one really made of?
case.question: What is each of Kai’s finds really made of?
case.how: Find 4 clues as you work through the lesson. Then crack the case (solve it) at the top of the Assignment tab.

clues.t: Looks can’t prove what a material is. Gold and fool’s gold look almost the same. Kai’s tags need TESTS.
The “SILVER” bolt is silver-gray, hard, magnetic and sinks. That fingerprint matches steel. Silver is NOT magnetic.

clues.where: The Lesson, Part 2: knock out the suspects
clues.t: The “old COIN” is gray, NOT magnetic and light for its size: aluminum. Gray alone left 5 suspects!

clues.where: The Lesson, Part 4: build your claim
clues.t: The “GOLD!” nugget has a greenish-black streak and weighs only 5 g: pyrite, fool’s gold. The “DIAMOND” weighs 2.5 g and leaves a white streak: glass.

solve.title: What did Kai really find?
solve.q: Which answer fits all four clues?

options.t: Gold, silver, a diamond and an old coin, just like his tags say.
options.why: Check Clue 1. Kai only looked. The tests tell a different story.

options.t: Fool’s gold (pyrite), a steel bolt, a piece of glass and an aluminum disc.
options.why: Case cracked! Every tag was wrong, and every answer has two or more tests behind it.

options.t: Fool’s gold, steel, glass and silver, because the coin is gray and shiny.
options.why: Check Clue 3. Silver is heavy for its size. The coin was light, so it’s aluminum.

options.t: Fool’s gold, silver, glass and iron, because every metal sticks to a magnet.
options.why: Check Clues 2 and 3. The bolt stuck, so it isn’t silver. The coin didn’t stick, and it’s still a metal.

tower.afterText: Is Kai’s nugget gold? Try to prove it.
tower.title: The claim tower

why.t: Something you say is true. A strong claim stands on evidence, like a tower on strong blocks.

todo: Look at the two nuggets.
Drag a block under Kai’s sign (or tap a block, then the tower).
Watch what happens. The 🔒 blocks are tests: you’ll run them in Part 3.

tower.startLine: Pick a block to hold up Kai’s sign.
tower.wobbleLine: Wobble! Blocks so far: {n}. Is it strong enough?
tower.fallLine: CRASH! Color, shine and Kai’s word can’t hold up the claim. Fool’s gold has all of those too. You need TESTS.

opts.t: Looks alone can’t prove what a material is.

opts.miss: It’s not the size of the blocks. Fool’s gold is gold-colored and shiny too!
It IS shiny. But so is fool’s gold. Shine can’t tell them apart.

tower.win: Looks can’t prove it. Tests can. Clue 1!

barcode.afterText: print the fingerprint of Kai’s “SILVER” bolt.
barcode.title: Fingerprint barcode

why.t: Its own set of properties. Two materials can share one or two, but the whole set is different, like your fingerprint.

todo: Run each test on the bolt. Then flip the switch to match.
Each switch prints a stripe.
Drag the strip over the shelf (or tap a card) until every stripe lines up.
barcode.printLine: Each switch you set prints a stripe.
barcode.slideLine: Drag the strip over a card on the shelf, or tap a card.

props.miss: Look again: what color did the test show?

props.result: No dent at all. It’s hard.
props.miss: Your fingernail couldn’t dent it. Is it hard?
The magnet grabbed it. Is it magnetic?

props.result: Plop. It sinks to the bottom.

shelf.why: So close! But the magnet stripe doesn’t match. Silver is NOT magnetic, and the bolt is.
Wood is brown, a fingernail can dent it, and it floats. Most stripes don’t match!
Every stripe lines up! The bolt is steel. Steel is mostly iron, so the magnet grabbed it.
The color stripe doesn’t match. Copper is orange-brown, and it isn’t magnetic.
Glass is clear, and a magnet doesn’t pull it.

barcode.q: Kai’s tag says SILVER. Which stripe proves it isn’t silver?

opts.t: The magnet stripe: silver isn’t magnetic, but the bolt is.

opts.miss: Both are silver-gray. Color can’t tell them apart!

knockout.afterText: Three or four properties together build a strong case.
knockout.title: Knock out the suspects

why.t: Each test rules some materials out. Keep testing until only one material fits ALL the evidence.

todo: Drag a test onto the board (or tap a test, then the board).
Every suspect that doesn’t match flips down.
Keep testing until ONE suspect is left.

tests.line: Every suspect that isn’t gray flips down. Look how many gray ones are left!
The magnetic ones flip down. Surprise: aluminum, silver, lead, copper and gold are metals too, and a magnet doesn’t pull any of them. Only iron, nickel and steel stick.
It weighs about one third as much as the same size of steel. The heavy suspects flip down.

knockout.noneLine: Nobody flipped down. That test can’t split the suspects that are left. Try another one.
knockout.q: Why did the color test leave so many suspects?

opts.t: Lots of different materials are gray.

opts.miss: Color is observable: you see it. And lots of materials share the same color.
Age doesn’t matter. Iron, nickel, aluminum, silver and lead are all gray.

knockout.win: The coin is aluminum: gray, not magnetic and light for its size. Clue 3!

streak.afterText: Time to run the tests that looking can’t do.
streak.title: The streak plate

why.t: The color of a mineral’s powder. Rub it on a rough white tile and look. The streak can be a different color than the mineral itself!

todo: Drag each nugget across the white tile (or tap a nugget, then the tile).
Then drag the steel nail onto each nugget.
Then weigh each one. Both pieces are the same size.

nuggets.streakLine: A greenish-black streak! Hmm. Is that what gold does?
nuggets.scratchLine: Screech… the nail slid right off. Not a scratch!
The nail left a scratch. Gold is soft!

streak.plateLine: Drag a nugget onto the white tile, or tap a nugget and then the tile.
streak.nailLine: Drag the nail onto a nugget, or tap the nail and then a nugget.
streak.scaleLine: Both pieces are the same size (a 1-centimeter cube). Drag one onto the scale, or tap it and then the scale.

reveal.alt: A real streak test on a white tile: a dark streak next to a small brassy cube.
Real gold flakes beside a gold-yellow streak on a dark tile.

streak.credit: Kai’s nugget (pyrite from Peru): James St. John, CC BY 2.0 · Museum gold nugget from Australia: James St. John, CC BY 2.0 · both via Wikimedia Commons · Pyrite streak plate: Ra’ike, CC BY-SA 3.0 · Gold streak: Ra’ike, CC BY-SA 3.0 DE · via Wikimedia Commons

opts.t: No. Its streak is dark, a nail can’t scratch it, and it’s too light. It’s pyrite: fool’s gold!

opts.miss: Remember the tower? Looks can’t prove it. Check the streak.
Real gold is soft. The nail scratched the museum gold, but not Kai’s nugget.

fact.q: Why is it called fool’s gold?
fact.t: During gold rushes, some miners found shiny pyrite and thought they were rich. A streak test would have told them the truth: gold leaves a gold-yellow streak, and pyrite leaves a dark one.

streak.win: Kai’s nugget is pyrite: fool’s gold!

claimtiles.afterText: Then build a claim for each one.
claimtiles.title: Build your claim

why.t: It names the material AND gives two pieces of evidence from tests. One clue alone could fit a lookalike.

todo: Drag a test onto a sample’s row (or tap a test, then the row). Run at least 3 tests on each sample.
Compare the results with the property guide.
Build a claim for each sample: drag tiles into the blanks.

samples.wrongWhy: Check the guide. Gold leaves a gold-yellow streak and weighs 19 g.
samples.keyLine: True, but gold could match that too. Add the streak, the nail or the weigh test.

samples.wrongWhy: Check the guide. A diamond weighs 3.5 g and leaves no streak.
samples.keyLine: True, but a diamond could match that too. The weigh test or the streak tells them apart.

samples.wrongWhy: Check the guide. Wood is brown and leaves no streak.
samples.keyLine: True, but wood matches that too. Add the color, the streak or the nail test.
samples.doneLine: Identified: {m}! Wood that burned in the fire.

guide.fp: gold-yellow · gold-yellow streak · a nail scratches it · 19 g
brassy yellow · greenish-black streak · a nail can’t scratch it · 5 g
clear · white streak · a nail can’t scratch it · 2.5 g
clear · no streak (it scratches the tile!) · 3.5 g
black · black streak · crumbles · floats · less than 1 g
brown · no streak · floats · less than 1 g

decoys.miss: Lots of materials are shiny. Use a test result from the table.
Kai only looked! Use a test result from the table.

claimtiles.waitLine: Run at least {n} tests on a sample. Then you can build its claim.
claimtiles.oneLine: That’s the same test twice. Use two different tests.
claimtiles.win: Three claims, each with two pieces of evidence. Clue 4!

ringtwist.title: The “silver” ring

why.t: Kai found a ring on the dock. “This one’s SILVER for sure!” Ranger Bell hands you a magnet.

todo: Bring the magnet to the ring.
Then decide: is it silver?
ringtwist.clingLine: CLICK! The magnet grabbed the ring.
ringtwist.q: Real silver is never pulled by a magnet. So what is the ring?

opts.t: Not silver. Probably steel with a silver-colored coating.

opts.miss: Shine can’t prove it. Silver doesn’t stick to magnets, and this ring did.
Gold isn’t magnetic either, and the ring isn’t gold-colored.

fact.t: Jewelers often start with a magnet. Real silver and real gold don’t stick. If a “silver” ring sticks, there’s iron or steel in it.

ringtwist.win: One magnet test, and the tag was wrong again!

mlabel.title: The museum label

why.t: Ranger Bell wants Kai’s fool’s gold in the nature center. A good museum label names the find and gives the evidence.

todo: Pick the name.
Pick two pieces of evidence.
Print the label.

opts.miss: Brass is made by people. Kai’s nugget came out of the ground.
Real gold is gold-colored too, so that can’t prove it.

opts.t: A steel nail can’t scratch it
Only 5 g, not 19 g like gold
A steel nail can’t scratch it

tool.name: Scratch kit
tool.teaser: A real geologist’s kit: find out how hard a mystery sample is.
tool.done: Tool of the Week: you used a real scratch kit.

why.t: Tools of known hardness. If a tool scratches a sample, the sample is softer than the tool. Geologists carry one into the field.

hardness.title: Scratch and see
todo: Drag a tool onto a sample (or tap the tool, then the sample).
Try every tool on every sample.
Then answer the question.
hardness.model: A model. Try a fingernail and a penny on a piece of chalk at home.

samples.band: Very soft: even a fingernail scratches it.
Soft: a penny scratches it, a fingernail can’t.
Hard: nothing in the kit scratches it.
Hard: nothing in the kit scratches it.

q.q: Real gold is soft: a copper penny scratches it. What did the kit show about Kai’s nugget?

opts.t: Nothing scratched it, so it’s much harder than gold.
opts.why: Right! Gold is soft. Pyrite is hard. One more piece of evidence that Kai found fool’s gold.
Look again: even the steel nail couldn’t scratch it.
Real gold is soft. A penny scratches it.

q1.A: Plastic isn’t hard and doesn’t sink. And this one is magnetic!
q1.B: Aluminum is silver-gray, but a magnet doesn’t pull it. Remember Kai’s coin?

q2.A: Properties don’t lie. But one property can match lots of materials.
q2.C: Tests aren’t expensive. Gray alone left 5 suspects!

q3.B: A guess isn’t evidence. Kai guessed GOLD!

hlCoach.title: Highlight like a scientist
tips: Highlight key words, not whole paragraphs.
If everything is yellow, nothing stands out. Aim for a few words in each paragraph.
Look for words that are explained.
Bold words, and words followed by “means”, “is called” or a meaning in ( ), are often worth saving.
Look for answers to the Big Question.
Ask yourself: which properties helped identify the material, and which ones could fool you?
“Because”, “so” and “first … then” show how ideas connect.
Yellow = important. Green = evidence I might use in my answer. Pink = something I wonder about.

practice.q: Practice: tap the 3 to 5 words that matter most in this sentence.
practice.text: One property can fool you, so scientists match three or four properties to a property guide.
practice.model: A scientist might highlight “one property can fool you” and “three or four properties”. Those words hold the big idea.

hlCoach.outside: This works in every subject. When you read anything, save the words that answer your question, and skip the rest.
